description: We are software engineering students with a strong background in low-level logic, optimization algorithms, and rigorous problem-solving. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are applying this same structured algorithmic mindset to Python, spatial data architecture, and geospatial processing. Our focus is to build an efficient, working prototype that turns raw data into tangible, real-world impact.
summary:
S.O.L.O. (Smart Observation Land Optimization), also known as Field Friend, is an agricultural decision-support platform developed for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026. It addresses the challenge of climate adaptation by connecting smallholder farmers, particularly in Angola and other vulnerable agricultural communities, with NASA Earth Observation data.

The platform transforms satellite observations from NASA POWER and other Earth observation sources into practical agricultural recommendations, helping farmers monitor weather conditions, estimate soil moisture, optimize irrigation, and plan regenerative crop rotations. It also introduces a carbon credit estimation system that uses satellite data and internationally recognized scientific methodologies to make the voluntary carbon market more accessible to smallholder farmers.

Designed for rural communities, S.O.L.O. prioritizes accessibility through simplified interfaces, audio guidance, high-contrast visuals, and lightweight performance for low-bandwidth connections.

By combining space technology, agricultural science, and financial inclusion, S.O.L.O. empowers farmers to make informed decisions, strengthen climate resilience, improve soil health, and explore new economic opportunities.
details:
S.O.L.O. (Smart Observation Land Optimization) is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform that transforms NASA Earth Observation data into practical insights for smallholder farmers. Initially focused on Angola, the platform combines satellite observations, agronomic models, and accessible technology to support climate-resilient farming.

The system retrieves agroclimatic data from NASA POWER, including temperature, precipitation, humidity, solar radiation, and wind speed. These observations power a series of agricultural tools, including a weather monitoring dashboard, a two-layer soil water balance model, and an interactive crop rotation simulator. Using the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation, the platform estimates reference evapotranspiration and soil water dynamics, helping farmers make better irrigation decisions and reduce water waste.

Another key innovation is its carbon credit estimation module. By combining land characteristics, regenerative agricultural practices, and satellite-based information, S.O.L.O. estimates potential soil carbon sequestration and its equivalent value in the voluntary carbon market. Its methodology incorporates IPCC guidelines, the Verra VM0042 framework, and a conservative 20% risk buffer.

The platform was developed using Next.js 16, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, Python, and FastAPI. The frontend follows a server-side rendering approach to improve performance and reduce data consumption, while the backend uses Hexagonal Architecture to ensure modularity, maintainability, and separation of concerns. Additional technologies include SQLAlchemy, SQLite, PostgreSQL/PostGIS, Google Earth Engine integration, and NASA POWER APIs.

What makes S.O.L.O. creative is its combination of space-based observations, agricultural decision support, regenerative farming, and financial inclusion in a single platform. Instead of exposing farmers to complex scientific datasets, it translates technical measurements into understandable recommendations and visual indicators. It also incorporates audio guidance, high-contrast interfaces, large interactive elements, and lightweight pages designed for older farmers and communities with limited digital literacy or unreliable 3G connectivity.

During development, our team considered the realities of smallholder agriculture, particularly climate variability, soil degradation, limited access to technical expertise, financial exclusion, regional crop suitability, and rural connectivity constraints. We also prioritized scientific transparency by distinguishing model-based estimates from direct satellite measurements and avoiding fabricated weather forecasts.

Our intended impact is to strengthen agricultural resilience, promote sustainable land management, reduce inefficient water use, restore soil fertility, and create opportunities for smallholder farmers to participate in the voluntary carbon market. Ultimately, S.O.L.O. aims to make the benefits of space technology more accessible to the people who need them most.
